These were then Gaussian blurred one pixel again and brightness and contrast adjusted as needed to illustrate the fluorescence. Finally, these small fields of view were cropped again to yield the images in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

### Measuring inbreeding coefficients using genetics

We used a high-throughput system to genotype the progeny from each cross. First, we crossed two parental populations to generate spore progeny as described above. In addition to placing the mixed haploid cells on SPAS, we also diluted a subset of the mix and plated it onto YEAS (YEA +45 mg/L adenine, histidine, leucine, lysine, and uracil). We genotyped the colonies that grew on that YEAS plate to measure the starting frequency of each parental strain in the cross. We plated the spores produced by the cross on YEAS and grew them at 32°C for 4 days. We picked the colonies using a Qpix 420 Colony Picking System and cultured them in YEL for 24 hr at 30°C in 96-well round-bottom plates (Axygen). We then used a Singer RoTor robot to spot the cultures to YNP dropout and YEAS drug plates and incubated them at 32°C for 3 days. We then imaged the plates using an S&P robotics SPImager with a Canon EOS Rebel T3i camera. We analyzed each picture using the subtract background feature in Fiji and assigned regions of interest to the 384 spots where cells were pinned. We then measured the average intensity of each spot and classified cells as grown or not by a heuristic threshold. We genotyped some cross progeny manually using standard techniques due to robot unavailability, with indistinguishable results. A single cross was considered as one biological replicate.

We then inferred the frequency of mating between cells of distinct genotypes based on the frequency of recombinant progeny using a combination of either two or three unlinked genetic markers. If mating was random, we expect the progeny to reflect Hardy-Weinberg expectations ($p^{2}+2p1-p+1-p^{2}=1$), where $p^{2}+1-p^{2}$ reflect the expected frequency of homozygotes and $2p(1-p)$ reflects the expected frequency of outcrossing. Homozygotes of either parental genotype can only produce offspring with the parental genotypes. If the two parental strains outcross to generate heterozygotes, they will make the parental genotypes and recombinant genotypes all in equal frequencies (2n total genotypes where n is the number of segregating markers). For our crosses with three markers, we therefore expected the true ‘observed’ frequency of progeny produced by outcrossing to be equal to the number of observed recombinants divided by 6/8. For our crosses with two unlinked markers, we divided by 2/4. We then calculated the inbreeding coefficient using the formula,

$$
F=1-\frac{the true observed fraction of progeny produced by outcrossing}{2p1-p}.
$$

### Zygote frequency expectation under inbreeding and different mating efficiencies

We calculated the expected zygote frequencies when isolates were mated with different isolates on SPA (see Measuring inbreeding coefficients by microscopy) using an additive model that incorporated mating efficiencies and inbreeding coefficients measured from the isogenic crosses. The model assumed that each strain contributes equally to the cross, and that they do not change their own mating in response to the mating partner.

We calculated the expected frequency of homozygotes for parental strain one as:

$$
=p^{2}+p1-pF_{I1}1-u_{s1},
$$

where the inbreeding coefficient is $F_{I1}$ and the mating efficiency is $1-u_{s1}$ for parental strain 1 ($s1$), considering its initial frequency $p$. The expected heterozygote frequency is:

$$
=2p1-p1- \frac{F_{I1}+F_{I2}}{2}1-\frac{u_{s1}+u_{s2}}{2}.
$$

The expected fraction of homozygotes for parental strain two is:

$$
=1-(Homozygote frequency strain  1+ Heterozygote frequency)
$$

### Calculating expected allele frequencies after sexual reproduction

To model the expected changes in allele frequencies in a randomly mating population over time, we used the equations described by Crow, 1991. For nonrandomly mating populations, we included the ‘$F$’ inbreeding coefficient in the equations, similar to Hartl and Clark, 2007. We assumed that wtf4 had a drive strength (‘$k$') of 0.98 based on experimental observations (Nuckolls et al., 2017). We assumed the control allele exhibited Mendelian transmission ($k$ = 0.5). Simulations for the spread of a driver in Figure 3 only considered drive and inbreeding coefficients. To simulate drive in fluorescent populations, the starting frequencies of each allele (i.e., ‘$p$’) were determined empirically for each experiment using either traditional genetic approaches or cytometry. Predicted values were calculated from each biological replicate (independent cross), composed of three technical replicates measured via cytometry per cross. We assumed all genotypes had equal fitness as haploids. For relative fitness of diploids, we assigned mCherry/mCherry homozygotes a fitness of $w_{11}=1$, regardless of whether they were EV/EV or wtf4/wtf4 homozygotes. In all but one cross (see below), we observed a fitness cost linked to the GFP alleles relative to mCherry alleles during sexual reproduction, regardless of wtf4. We therefore used our data (see below) to calculate 0.234 as the fitness cost of the GFP-linked variant. Because of that, we assigned a fitness value of 0.766 to GFP homozygotes, $w_{22}$ . We found the fitness cost linked to GFP had low dominance (see below) and thus assigned a fitness value of 0.98 for GFP/mCherry homozygous for wtf4 or empty vector, $w_{12}$ . For GFP/mCherry heterozygotes that were also heterozygous for wtf4, we assigned a fitness of (0.5) that accounts for the death of spores killed by drive (0.51) and the GFP cost (0.234) and dominance (0.083).

The calculation for allele frequency for a wtf meiotic driver in consecutive sexual cycles from haploid populations is:

$$
p_{g+1}=\frac{p^{2}_{g}+Fp_{g}(1-p)_{g}w_{11}+2p_{g}1-p_{g}k(1-F)w_{12}}{W-_{g}}.
$$

where the mean fitness of the population at each generation ($g)$

$$
W-_{g}=p^{2}_{g}w_{11}+2p_{g}1-p_{g}w_{12}+(1-p)^{2}_{g}w_{22}+Fp_{g}1-p_{g}w_{11}+w_{22}-2w_{12}.
$$

When the fitness reduction in heterozygotes is only due to dead cells by drive with no additional costs, $w_{12}=\frac{1}{2k}$ , the drivers spread under any initial frequency greater than 0 (Crow, 1991).

To determine the fitness cost of the GFP-linked variant that was present in most of our experiments, we used the L-BFGS-B algorithm to find a fitness that maximized the likelihood that our observed allele frequencies varied only due to the linked cost of GFP ($c$) and dominance ($h$) in the first six generations of the control experiments shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2 (Byrd et al., 1995). To do this, we used the mle function from the R stats4 package (Team, 2019). We assumed the fitness cost alters the relative fitness of both homozygotes $w_{22}=1-c$ and heterozygotes $w_{12}=1-ch$. The fitting was done using only the initial six generations due to a rapid loss of fluorescent cells from seven to ten generations (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).

To calculate the minimum initial frequency of driver required to spread in a population when linked to alleles with varying additional fitness costs, we use the additional linked cost ($c)$ and their dominance ($h$) associated to each genotype and solved using (Wolfram, 1987). For simplicity we also assumed complete transmission bias, $k=1$. A wtf meiotic driver linked to a deleterious allele can spread under the condition (critical value) that

$$
F_{critical}<\frac{ch(p−1)−cp+p}{c(h−1)(p−1)+p}.
$$

where $p$ is the initial frequency of a wtf driver, c is the cost linked to the driver, and h is the dominance coefficient. For this case the assigned relative fitness for homozygote carrying the wtf driver is $w_{11}=1-c$.

### Modeling driver success in finite populations

To determine the possibility of a meiotic driver to spread and be fixed in a finite population, we ran stochastic simulations using a Wright-Fisher model considering multiple population sizes. We assumed no fitness differences between genotypes during haploid cell growth, complete drive (k = 1), gamete killing proportional to drive in heterozygotes, no linked deleterious alleles, and non-overlapping generations. We used characters of ‘0’ for non-driving cells and ‘1’ for driving cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B). Initially the population starts with population size (N). We next sampled a fixed population size (n) with replacement, assuming infinite gamete supply used for mating (e.g., as if mitotic expansion of the population occurred prior to mating). In our simulations N = n. We sampled mating groups without replacement for an inbreeding population (Spop) with a fraction F and the rest of cells (n − Spop) mate randomly. Populations that mate randomly are proportional to Hardy-Weinberg genotype frequencies with approximated integer values. Homozygotes (‘0,0’ and ‘1,1’) produce four progeny (‘0,0,0,0’ and ‘1,1,1,1’, respectively), while heterozygotes produce two progeny that inherit the drive allele (‘1,1’). When a fitness cost is associated with a genotype, we decimated the gametic products in proportion to the cost. The collection of 0’s and 1’s after this process constituted the next generation. We repeated 1000 generations for 1000 iterations for each tested condition.

### Measuring allele frequencies for experimental evolution analyses

We performed the crosses and collected spores as described above. We then started the next generation by culturing 60 µL of spores from each cross in each of three different wells with 600 µL fresh YEL media in 96 deep-well-round-bottom plates (Axygen) and cultured for 24 hr at 1200 rpm at 32°C. We then transferred 60 µL from each culture to a new plate with 600 µL YEL and cultured for 12–14 hr at 1200 rpm at 32°C. We then pooled the culture replicates in an Eppendorf tube, spun down, and resuspended them in an equal volume of ddH2O. We then took 100 µL of this sample to assay via cytometry (described below). We also plated 200 µL of each sample on SPAS plates and incubated at 25°C for 5 days to allow the cells to mate and sporulate.

To detect and quantify fluorescent cells via flow cytometry, we used the ZE5 Cell Analyzer (Bio-Rad). We spun down 100 µL of each culture, washed the cell pellet with water, spun down again, and resuspended the cells in 200 µL of 1× PBS (phosphate buffered saline) with 1.5 μL 4′,6-diamidino-2-phenylindole (DAPI, Sigma-Aldrich, 100 ng/mL). DAPI stains dead cells, so we considered DAPI-negative cells as live cells. To image DAPI, we used 355 nm laser excitation and a 447/60 nm detector. To image GFP, we excited using a 488 nm laser and detected emission with a 525/35 nm filter. To image mCherry, we excited using a 561 nm laser and detected emission with a 615/24 nm filter. We used 405 and 488 nm (FSC 405 and FSC 488) lasers for forward scatter and 488 nm laser for side scatter (SSC 488).

To quantify the frequency of GFP- or mCherry-positive cells, we analyzed the Flow Cytometry Standard files in R/Bioconductor using the packages FlowTrans and FlowClust (Lo et al., 2009). We first separated the cells that had round and uniform shape and similar granularity. This step allowed us to detect a more uniform population of single cells. We then discarded DAPI-positive cells. To determine the GFP- and mCherry-positive cells, we used limits for each channel. The limits varied throughout the experiment due to reconfiguration in the flow cytometer. For every measurement, we corrected with standard samples of cells that only expressed either GFP or mCherry. Fluorescent GFP- and mCherry-positive cells always showed non-overlapping cell populations. We quantified cells that were not classified as non-fluorescent cells.

### Fluorescent marker loss in experimental evolution

In the experimental evolution experiments (Figures 4 and 5B, and Figure 4—figure supplement 2), a large proportion of cells lost their fluorescent marker over time (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A-B). We assume this is because we introduced the markers using an integrating plasmid that enters the genome following a single crossover event. Because of this, a single crossover can then pop the marker and the associated vector out of the genome. We repeatedly observed that the loss occurred faster with the mCherry markers. Consistent with this model, cells that lost fluorescence generally also lost the associated drug resistance marker present on the integrating vector.

We only considered fluorescent cells in our analyses. In the experiments (Figure 4B–C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A-B, and Figure 5B), we extended the evolution up to 10 generations. In other experiments (Figure 4D–E and Figure 4—figure supplement 2C-D), we removed non-fluorescent cells by cell sorting after generations 2 and 5. To sort cells, we first collected and cultured spores as described above with the first culture done for 12 hr. We then transferred 60 µL of germinated cells into 600 µL fresh YEL media. We used three cultures for each experimental line and pooled all in equal amounts to have 1.4 mL of each line. We spun each sample down and resuspended the cells in 5 mL ddH2O prior to sorting. We removed non-fluorescent cells and retained GFP-positive (488 nm laser for excitation and a filter 507 nm) and mCherry-positive (561 nm laser for excitation and a 582 nm filter) cells using the laser the BD FACSMelody cell sorter software. We collected 1.2 million cells for each line into 1× PBS. We then spun down the cells and resuspended the pellets in 200 µL YEL. We then took 60 µL from each sample and diluted the cells into 600 µL YEL and continued with the time course as described above. This restored fluorescently labeled cells populations as expected for homothallic and heterothallic lines (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B). Cell sorting did not affect our results as we observed the same patterns in replicate experiments in which we did not remove the non-fluorescent cells (Figure 4).

Meiotic drivers are selfish elements that distort segregation to be over-represented in offspring of heterozygotes. Multiple meiotic drive elements are known in the yeast Schizosaccharomyces pombe, S. pombe, which can seem puzzling as this fungus has long been thought to undergo little outcrossing. This manuscript reports theoretical and experimental analyses suggesting that the outcrossing rate can be high enough in this species to explain the spread of multiple meiotic drive elements. The findings support the emerging view that homothallic fungi can undergo quite high rates of outcrossing, which is also in agreement with evolutionary considerations on the evolution of mating types. This study can thus be of high relevance for scientists studying meiotic drivers and/or mating systems and their evolution.

Reviewer #1 (Recommendations for the authors):

The whole introduction is based on the rationale that homothallism means selfing while heterothallism means outcrossing. There are several issues with such assumptions. First selfing and outcrossing will be understood by most readers of eLife as “diploid selfing/outcrossing”, as in plants and animals, while heterothallism does not prevent diploid selfing, and actually many heterothallic fungi undergo mostly diploid selfing (e.g. Microbotryum violacem, Neurospora tetrasperma, Podospora anserina). Conversely, homothallism does not prevent outcrossing and may not even have evolved to facilitated inbreeding but instead the opposite, universal compatibility under outcrossing. See below some references discussing these issues and some references showing that homothallic fungi do outcross and that many heterothallic fungi do self a lot. I would therefore not consider particularly surprising that S. pombe outcross enough for meiotic drivers to spread, although this indeed goes against the current view, based on the misconceptions above. The only good way to estimate outcrossing rates is by using population genetics or genomics on natural populations, as experiments will likely fail to mimic natural dispersal or conditions of mating. This is briefly discussed in the discussion but the whole introduction is misleading in my opinion. I understand this is a quite frequent view among scientists working on fungi (as they infer rates based on what they observe in Petri dishes and were often not evolutionary biologists), but the authors precisely miss the opportunity to state that this view is likely incorrect and to explain why, as this is precisely what they show. I did not understand why outcrossing in natural populations in S. pombe has not been estimated or at least discussed based on the genomic data in Jeffares et al. 2015. I think that framing the study into this evolutionary context will only make it stronger. I would also recommend to highlight much more the variation in the propensity of inbreeding among natural isolates and the existence of heterothallic strains. Is it frequently the case in nature?

Reviewer #2 (Recommendations for the authors):

As it stands, the population genetic modeling (Main Text lines 315-339, Methods lines 727-773, Figures3,5A) is used mainly to generate frequency trajectories of meiotic drivers against which the trajectories observed in the evolution experiments (Figures4,5B) can be compared. Of course, the similarity of the predicted and experimentally observed trajectories is exciting – I suspect that, based on results like these, pombe will soon become (if it is not already) the premier experimental system for meiotic drive. Still, it seems a missed opportunity, given the variation in mating behavior across strains that the authors have so carefully documented, not to use the population genetic modeling to link this variation with (perhaps even immediately testable) predictions about the natural history of drive in pombe. Below, I suggest some directions in which this might be achieved.

– The authors focus on the effect of inbreeding on the spread of a driver that starts at an appreciable frequency in the population (e.g., 5%, as in Figure 3B). They find that, while inbreeding slows down the spread of a driver from such frequencies, it does not prevent the driver's eventual spread to fixation. Based on this result, a reader might naively infer that inbreeding affects only the transient dynamics of meiotic drive, not whether a driver spreads to fixation or not; and therefore that strains with different levels of inbreeding will not necessarily have different numbers of fixed drivers.

However, a new driver appears by mutation as a single copy at its locus, and from this starting point, the driver's spread to fixation is not guaranteed – indeed, in the case of spore killers in fungi, it is always unlikely (Martinossi-Allibert et al. 2021). The probability that the driver will go on to achieve an appreciable frequency in the population (and therefore eventually to fix) is governed by the interplay between random stochastic drift at low copy numbers of the driver and the deterministic advantage enjoyed by the driver. Since the latter depends strongly on the degree of inbreeding, inbreeding will substantially affect the fixation probability, and therefore the substitution rate, of meiotic drivers in the various strains studied by the authors. For example, if outcrossing occurs once every 100,000 generations, then a driver starting at low copy number is subject to ~100,000 generations of random drift before it can benefit from its transmission advantage; in this long interval, the driver is very likely to have drifted to extinction. In contrast, in a strain that outcrosses every generation, a newly arisen driver exercises its transmission advantage immediately and regularly, and therefore has a much higher chance of escaping stochastic loss.

I believe that questions like these could be investigated using the authors' population genetic model simply by simulating stochastic versions of this model – say, under a Wright-Fisher process – and starting the simulations with a single copy of the driver. This exercise would, I suspect, yield potentially testable predictions about variation in the number of fixed wtf drivers across different strains. Of course, these predictions would be "all else equal", but it would nevertheless be interesting just to see – given that strains do vary in the number of fixed wtf drivers (lines 490-491) – whether strains with lower levels of inbreeding harbor more fixed drivers.

– Turning to the transient dynamics of drivers on their way to fixation, it is striking in Figure 3B just how severely inbreeding affects the time required for fixation of a driver. It seems that the trajectories should be "stretched" according to the number of generations until each outcrossing event. Thus, in a strain that outcrosses once every 100,000 generations, a driver will take ~100,000x more generations to fix than it would in a strain that outcrosses every generation. This yields the prediction that, in strains with higher levels of inbreeding, although there should be fewer drivers fixed or spreading towards fixation (above), a greater fraction of these drivers should still be on their way to fixation, relative to a strain with lower levels of inbreeding. I.e., a greater fraction of drivers should still be polymorphic in strains that inbreed more frequently. (This prediction depends, I think, on the rate of appearance of drivers in the population relative to the average time a driver takes to fix.)

Empirically, are polymorphisms ever observed for wtf drivers? If not, why not? If so, do strains differ in the fraction of driver loci that are polymorphic vs fixed? If the answers to these questions are interesting, the authors might wish to use stochastic simulations of their population genetic model to obtain a more precise understanding of the predicted differences in polymorphism across strains.

– Finally, it has recently been suggested that, owing to inbreeding's effect in slowing the spread of meiotic drivers, the presence of meiotic drivers in a species might conversely select for greater degrees of inbreeding (Bull 2017). This selective force would appear to be especially strong in pombe, in which drivers are both pervasive and highly destructive. Perhaps the authors could discuss whether they believe that mating behavior across strains of pombe (and perhaps further afield) have been shaped by meiotic drivers?

Reviewer #1 (Recommendations for the authors):

I found the manuscript much improved, and the additional analyses interesting.

However, I think that the use of “inbreeding” and “outcrossing” are still unclear and misleading. Many readers will just read this as typical inbreeding and outcrossing in plants and animals while the phenomena here are completely different. In addition, you sometimes use “outcrossing” as true outcrossing (eg L94, L114) and at many places one wonders in what sense you use the terms (in particular iin the model part). Science should use exact terms and avoid confusion and ambiguity. I think that “inbreeding” should be replaced by “same-clone mating” and “outcrossing” by something like “non-same-clone mating”. In addition, as said in my previous review, more emphasis should be put on the high rate of non-same-clone mating in homothallics, and how this goes against the (wrong) view in the fungal literature ; this is what is important for the spread of drivers. The emphasis is currently put on the lower rate of non-same-clone mating in heterothallics which is just its definition. These question should be specifically written in the introduction, refering to previous publication showing that homothallics do outcross (e.g., 10.1038/hdy.2014.37). The discussion should also more explicitly discuss the fact that, in natural conditions, dispersal may promote further non-same-clone mating and (true) outcrossing.

In addition, I found the answer to the previous comment below not convincing, this should be more explicitly discussed : “This method introduces a bias towards the correlation switching and selfing, because the latter is used as a proxy for the first.”

Reviewer #2 (Recommendations for the authors):

The authors have addressed my previous comments, in some cases carrying out interesting new analyses that have improved the manuscript. I appreciate that some of the questions raised in my previous report concerning the long-term population genetics of drive in pombe are beyond the scope of the present work, though I encourage the authors to consider these questions in future work since they are, I think, "within reach" and would lead to greater understanding of the fantastic system this group is developing.

Reviewer #3 (Recommendations for the authors):

The revision of the authors has greatly improved the manuscript and has removed most of the questions I had placed with the previous version. The logic of the interaction between switching frequency, outcrossing and population dynamics are better explained and caveats to the conclusions are addressed. The addition of the information on the multiallelic wtf genes also helps with understanding how allele frequencies change over time and that an established allele does not mean fixation. Below a few additional comments on the new manuscript and some elaborations on my previous comments.

The authors have chosen to consistently use the term selfing to describe same clone mating. Even though they clearly define the use of their term, I disagree with this choice. To a population geneticist or evolutionary biologist this is confusing. The term 'same clone mating' is unambiguous and would be preferred.

It is unfortunate that direct measurements of mating types was not possible. Though sad that this effort was unsuccessful, it is personally comforting to hear, as in our hands tracking of switching using fluorescent markers has also been unsuccessful. It would be great if a measure would be possible and hopefully a good method will become available to directly assess switching.

From the reply to my comments 5 and 6 it is clear I did not express myself clearly. Specifically, the use of the fitness costs or benefits of the driving allele are not interpreted as I meant them. Let me elaborate on this. There are different moments where a cost can be incurred during the lifecycle of fission yeast. First during the haploid phase (e.g. germination, haploid mitosis), during mating and at the diploid phase (e.g. diploid mitosis, meiosis, sporogenesis). The fitness in the haploid phase (not modelled by the authors) is likely based on the genome of the individual, whereas mating and the diploid phase are affected by the two genomes. When I refer to the fitness cost/benefit, I always refer to the effect on an allele, as this is the unit of inheritance (similar to the change in p modelled by the authors). The 'cost of a driver' would be the negative effect the allele has on its reproduction, either during the haploid or diploid phase (changing w22 and/or w12 in the model). Killing per se is not a cost to the driver, as it does not reduce its own survival when heterozygous, it only affects the wild type allele. There is a cost to the diploid individual (fitness = 0.5), causing genomic conflict, but under full drive (k=1) this does not affect the driving allele and is thus not a cost to this allele. Drivers can become associated with deleterious mutations due to suppressed recombination, gene disruptions etc. as the authors also mention in line 599, however, to my knowledge such genetic associations have not been described in fission yeast. It might be good to explicitly mention the situation for fission yeast.

Also no reduction in haploid or diploid growth rate has been shown for drivers, or at least not for wtf4 ("Outside of its role in meiotic drive, wtf4 has no apparent role in promoting fertility", pp. 13 Nuckolis et al. 2017) and therefore I consider these driving alleles neutral.

I asked before if there could be a direct benefit to driving alleles. The most obvious would be a benefit to germination rate/ spore survival due to potential resource allocation from the killed spores to the killers. This could improve fitness during the haploid phase (w1 > w2), thereby increasing the allele frequency of the drivers before the next sexual phase. Such secondary effects of killing could greatly speed up the initial phase of invasion when the driver's frequency is low and killing thus slow, which helps to overcome the selection-drift barrier.

Staying with drift. It is nice to see the extension of the model using different population sizes (lines 500-512; Figure S3c). The results that show that drivers have a higher chance of establishment in smaller populations fit with prediction from the Wright-Fisher model where chance of fixation is directly proportional to the allele frequency. With smaller populations, the initial allele frequency increases (1/N) reducing the chance of loss by drift. It is not clear to me how the "local patch" dynamics as discussed in lines 741-746 affects the dynamics at the population level, where the allele frequencies of all the local patches are combined resulting in the initial population with large population sizes. If there is some form of population structure, of which there is probably some (Jeffares et al. 2015, Tusso et al. 2019) the allele frequencies might locally become higher increasing the chance of establishment of novel alleles. It would be interesting to see how multiple small demes with migration might affect speed of invasion and might affect dynamics of multiple drivers.

claims.source: Heterothallic S. pombe strains must mate with non-clonally related cells of the opposite mating type to complete sexual reproduction (Egel, 1977; Gutz and Doe, 1975; Leupold, 1949; Miyata and Miyata, 1981; Nieuwenhuis and Immler, 2016; Osterwalder, 1924; Schlake and Gutz, 1993).
claims.evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claims.claim: Most isolates of S. pombe are homothallic, meaning they can switch between the two mating types during clonal expansion via mitosis.
claims.source: However, most isolates of S. pombe are homothallic, that is, they can switch between the two mating types (h+ and h-) during clonal expansion via mitosis (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B; Egel and Eie, 1987; Gutz and Doe, 1975; Klar, 1990; Nieuwenhuis et al., 2018; Singh and Klar, 2003).
claims.evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work and a figure.

claims.claim: Homothallism in S. pombe enables mating to occur between cells clonally derived from the same progenitor via mitosis.
claims.source: Homothallism in S. pombe enables mating to occur between cells clonally derived from the same progenitor via mitosis (Billiard et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claims.claim: Mating in S. pombe can occur between two cells produced by a single mitotic cell division.
claims.source: Mating can even occur between two cells produced by a single mitotic cell division (Egel, 1977; Gutz and Doe, 1975; Miyata and Miyata, 1981).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: Homothallism in fungi does not inherently lead to mating between clonally related cells.
claims.source: It is important to note, however, that homothallism in fungi does not inherently lead to mating between clonally related cells (Giraud et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claims.claim: Under some conditions, homothallism can be a beneficial strategy for outcrossing species as it ensures gamete compatibility.
claims.source: Under some conditions, such as when gametes are dispersed and finding a mate is costly, homothallism can be a beneficial strategy for outcrossing species as it ensures gamete compatibility (Billiard et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claims.claim: Population genetic analyses of Sclerotinia sclerotiorum support that homothallism is compatible with frequent outcrossing.
claims.source: In addition, population genetic analyses of one homothallic fungus, Sclerotinia sclerotiorum, support that homothallism is compatible with frequent outcrossing (Attanayake et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claims.claim: Very little is known about the ecology of S. pombe in the wild, including how often S. pombe cells outcross.
claims.source: Very little is known about the ecology of S. pombe in the wild, including how often S. pombe cells outcross (Jeffares, 2018).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claims.claim: Outcrossing homothallic Sp strains is significantly more challenging than crossing heterothallic isolates.
claims.source: Distinct homothallic Sp strains can be induced to mate in the lab (i.e., outcrossed), but such crosses are significantly more challenging to execute than crosses between heterothallic isolates.
claims.evidence: This is based on established laboratory knowledge.

claims.claim: The relative difficulty associated with outcrossing homothallic strains has been attributed to preferential same-clone mating.
claims.source: The relative difficulty associated with outcrossing homothallic strains has been attributed to preferential same-clone mating (Ekwall and Thon, 2017; Forsburg and Rhind, 2006).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: Microscopy experiments have supported the idea that homothallic Sp haploids tend to undergo same-clone mating.
claims.source: Microscopy experiments have supported the idea that homothallic Sp haploids tend to undergo same-clone mating (Bendezú and Martin, 2013; Egel, 1977; Leupold, 1949; Miyata and Miyata, 1981).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: The precise level of same-clone mating when homothallic S. pombe cells are among nonclonal sexual partners has not been formally reported for any isolate.
claims.source: However, the precise level of same-clone mating when homothallic S. pombe cells are among nonclonal sexual partners has not, to our knowledge, been formally reported for any isolate.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the lack of previous quantitative data.

claims.claim: There are two major S. pombe lineages that diverged between 2300 and 78,000 years ago.
claims.source: There are two major S. pombe lineages that diverged between 2300 and 78,000 years ago (Tao et al., 2019; Tusso et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: Much of the sampled variation within S. pombe represents different admixed hybrids of two ancestral lineages resulting from an estimated 20–60 outcrossing events.
claims.source: Much of the sampled variation within the species represents different admixed hybrids of those two ancestral lineages resulting from an estimated 20–60 outcrossing events (Tusso et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claims.claim: Outcrossing rate estimates in S. pombe are likely low because pervasive meiotic drive and decreased recombination in heterozygotes suppress the genetic signatures used to infer outcrossing.
claims.source: It is important to note, however, that the outcrossing rate estimates in S. pombe are likely low as pervasive meiotic drive and decreased recombination in heterozygotes suppress the genetic signatures that are used to infer outcrossing (Bravo Núñez et al., 2020b; Hu et al., 2017; Nuckolls et al., 2017; Zanders et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: More than four drivers and more than eight suppressors of drive could be present in a given heterozygote produced by outcrossing in S. pombe.
claims.source: First, the landscape of meiotic drivers and their suppressors is complex in that more than four drivers and more than eight suppressors of drive could be present in a given heterozygote produced by outcrossing (Eickbush et al., 2019; Bravo Núñez et al., 2020a).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: S. pombe isolates contain an array of chromosomal rearrangements and other unknown barriers to recombination.
claims.source: In addition to the drivers, S. pombe isolates contain an array of chromosomal rearrangements and other unknown barriers to recombination (Avelar et al., 2013; Brown et al., 2011; Jeffares et al., 2017; Tusso et al., 2019; Zanders et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: The presence of drivers affects the recombination rate within viable offspring, independent of chromosomal rearrangements.
claims.source: Importantly, recombination rates are also inextricably linked to the complex drive landscape because the presence of drivers also affects the recombination rate within viable offspring, independent of chromosomal rearrangements (Bravo Núñez et al., 2020b).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claims.claim: The notion that S. pombe infrequently outcrosses has been used to challenge the idea that S. pombe meiotic drivers are truly selfish genes that persist due to meiotic drive.
claims.source: In fact, the notion that S. pombe infrequently outcrosses has even been used to challenge the idea that S. pombe meiotic drivers are truly selfish genes that persist due to meiotic drive (Sweigart et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claims.claim: The S. pombe genome houses numerous meiotic drive genes from the wtf gene family.
claims.source: Nonetheless, the S. pombe genome houses numerous meiotic drive genes from the wtf gene family (Bravo Núñez et al., 2018; Bravo Núñez et al., 2020a; Eickbush et al., 2019; Hu et al., 2017; Nuckolls et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: Each wtf drive gene encodes both a Wtfpoison and a Wtfantidote protein that execute targeted killing of spores that do not inherit the wtf driver.
claims.source: Each wtf drive gene encodes both a Wtfpoison and a Wtfantidote protein that, together, execute targeted killing of the spores that do not inherit the wtf driver (Hu et al., 2017; Nuckolls et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: The Wtf4poison protein assembles into toxic protein aggregates that are packaged into all developing spores.
claims.source: In the characterized wtf4 driver, the Wtf4poison protein assembles into toxic protein aggregates that are packaged into all developing spores.
claims.evidence: This is based on previous characterization of wtf4.

claims.claim: The Wtf4antidote protein co-assembles with Wtf4poison only in spores that inherit wtf4 and likely neutralizes the poison by promoting its trafficking to the vacuole.
claims.source: The Wtf4antidote protein co-assembles with Wtf4poison only in the spores that inherit wtf4 and likely neutralizes the poison by promoting its trafficking to the vacuole (Nuckolls et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claims.claim: Spore killing by wtf drivers leads to the loss of about half of the spores and almost exclusive transmission (>90%) of the wtf driver from a heterozygote.
claims.source: Spore killing by wtf drivers leads to the loss of about half of the spores and almost exclusive transmission (>90%) of the wtf driver from a heterozygote (Hu et al., 2017; Nuckolls et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: All assayed S. pombe isolates contain multiple wtf drivers (4–14 drivers).
claims.source: Despite their heavy costs to the fitness of heterozygotes, the drivers are successful in that all assayed S. pombe isolates contain multiple wtf drivers (4–14 drivers; Bravo Núñez et al., 2020a; Eickbush et al., 2019; Hu et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: S. pombe isolates contain between 8 and 17 suppressors of drive that encode only a Wtfantidote protein.
claims.source: In addition to those drivers, the S. pombe isolates also contain between 8 and 17 suppressors of drive that encode only a Wtfantidote protein.
claims.evidence: This is based on previous characterization of S. pombe isolates.

claims.claim: In homothallic Sp cells, the average inbreeding coefficient measured using microscopy assay was 0.57.
claims.source: In homothallic cells of the common lab isolate, Sp, we measured an average inbreeding coefficient of 0.57 using our microscopy assay (Figure 1B and D).
claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data in Figure 1.

claims.claim: A mixed heterothallic population containing roughly equal amounts of GFP-expressing and mCherry-expressing cells of both mating types exhibited random mating (F = −0.05).
claims.source: We did observe random mating of this mixed heterothallic population (F = −0.05), which helps validate our assay (Figure 1D).
claims.evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by data in Figure 1D.

claims.claim: The average inbreeding coefficients measured using the genetic assay for homothallic Sp cells was 0.49.
claims.source: The average inbreeding coefficients measured using the genetic assay were very similar to the values we measured using the microscopy assay (0.49 for homothallic Sp cells; Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
claims.evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claims.claim: Measured inbreeding coefficients varied significantly between different S. pombe natural isolates.
claims.source: We found that the measured inbreeding coefficients varied significantly between the different natural isolates (Figure 1D).
claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data in Figure 1D.

claims.claim: Mating efficiency varied among S. pombe natural isolates, ranging from 10% in FY28981 to 50% in Sk.
claims.source: We also observed variation in mating efficiency ranging from 10% of cells mating in FY28981 to 50% of cells mating in Sk (Figure 1E).
claims.evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by data in Figure 1E.

claims.claim: Inbreeding coefficients were higher in both Sp and Sk isolates when cell densities were lower.
claims.source: We found that inbreeding coefficients were higher in both Sp and Sk isolates when cell densities were lower (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C and D).
claims.evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C and D.

claims.claim: Cells plated at low density tended to be physically distant from potential sexual partners that were not part of the same clonally growing patch of cells.
claims.source: This is likely because cells plated at low density tended to be physically distant from potential sexual partners that were not part of the same clonally growing patch of cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on experimental observations shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claims.claim: A control population of mixed heterothallic Sp cells showed near random mating between two genotypes at all cell densities assayed.
claims.source: However, a control population consisting of mixed heterothallic Sp cells (h+ and h- cells of two different genotypes mixed in equal proportions) that cannot mate within a clonal patch of cells showed near random mating between the two genotypes at all cell densities assayed (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C).
claims.evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C.

claims.claim: Sk cells plated at 0.25× density on SPA divided significantly more than Sp cells prior to the first mating.
claims.source: Sk cells plated at 0.25× density on SPA divided significantly more than Sp cells prior to the first mating (Wilcox rank sum test; p < 0.005 Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by data in Figure 2B and statistical analysis.

claims.claim: Sk progenitor cells most frequently started mating at the fourth mitotic generation.
claims.source: Sk progenitor cells most frequently started mating at the fourth mitotic generation (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by data in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: Many mating events in Sk were between non-sibling cells.
claims.source: In addition, many mating events were between non-sibling cells.
claims.evidence: This is an experimental observation from time-lapse imaging.

claims.claim: An ~5 kb insertion of nested Tf transposon sequences was found in the Sk mating-type region.
claims.source: However, using a previously published mate-pair sequencing dataset, we discovered an ~5 kb insertion of nested Tf transposon sequences in the Sk mating-type region (Eickbush et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from analysis of sequencing data, supported by a citation.

claims.claim: The ~5 kb insertion in the Sk mating-type region was confirmed using PCR.
claims.source: We confirmed the presence of the insertion using PCR (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A-B).
claims.evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A-B.

claims.claim: Evidence consistent with the same insertion was found in FY28981.
claims.source: We also found evidence consistent with the same insertion in FY28981, which also mates more randomly than Sp (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B, Figure 1D).
claims.evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B.

claims.claim: At 1× density, Sk cells generally mated in the second and third mitotic generations, like Sp.
claims.source: Whereas Sk cells tended to first mate in the fourth generation at 0.25× density, at 1× density Sk cells, like Sp, generally mated in the second and third mitotic generations (Figure 2C, Figure 2—video 2 supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by data in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: Significantly reduced levels of mating between Sk sibling cells were observed at 1× density relative to 0.25× (10% and 56%, respectively).
claims.source: Additionally, we observed significantly reduced levels of mating between Sk sibling cells at 1× density relative to 0.25× (10% and 56%, respectively; Figure 2E and B).
claims.evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by data in Figure 2E and B.

claims.claim: The Sk natural isolate displayed tremendous diversity in ascus size and shape.
claims.source: While assaying inbreeding cytologically, we noticed that the Sk natural isolate displayed tremendous diversity in ascus size and shape (Figure 1C, Figure 2—figure supplement 3A, Figure 2—video 2).
claims.evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by figures and videos.

claims.claim: Most S. pombe isolates generated zygotes or asci that were ~10–15 μm.
claims.source: We found that most isolates generated zygotes or asci that were ~10–15 μm, similar to Sp.
claims.evidence: This is an experimental finding from measuring ascus length.

claims.claim: ~25% of Sk zygotes and asci were longer than 15 μm, with some exceeding 30 μm.
claims.source: The majority of Sk zygotes and asci also fell within this range, but ~25% of Sk zygotes and asci were longer than 15 μm, with some exceeding 30 μm (Figure 2—figure supplement 3C).
claims.evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 3C.

claims.claim: Sk produced long shmoos only in response to cells of the opposite mating type and not as a response to nitrogen starvation alone.
claims.source: Sk produced long shmoos only in response to cells of the opposite mating type and not as a response to nitrogen starvation alone (Figure 2—figure supplement 3B).
claims.evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 3B.

claims.claim: The overall inbreeding coefficient of the mixed Sk/Sp population of cells was intermediate between single-isolate crosses and mixed crosses.
claims.source: We observed in experiments employing still images that the overall inbreeding coefficient of the mixed Sk/Sp population of cells was intermediate between single-isolate crosses and mixed crosses (Figure 2D).
claims.evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by data in Figure 2D.

claims.claim: Sk cells maintained low levels of mating between sibling cells in the mixed Sk/Sp population (9.2% compared to 9.8% in a homogeneous population).
claims.source: In time-lapse experiments, we observed that Sk cells maintained low levels of mating between sibling cells in the mixed Sk/Sp population (9.2% compared to 9.8% in a homogeneous population; Figure 2E).
claims.evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by data in Figure 2E.

claims.claim: Among Sp cells, mating between sibling cells decreased significantly from 56.8% to 29.7% in the mixed mating environment.
claims.source: Among the Sp cells, mating between sibling cells decreased significantly from 56.8% to 29.7% in the mixed mating environment (Figure 2E; t-test, p = 0.04).
claims.evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by data in Figure 2E and statistical analysis.

claims.claim: Sk/Sp matings produce significantly longer zygotes/asci than either Sk/Sk or Sp/Sp matings.
claims.source: We did, however, find that Sk/Sp matings produce significantly longer zygotes/asci than either Sk/Sk or Sp/Sp matings (Figure 2—figure supplement 4B).
claims.evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 4B.

claims.claim: The wtf driver has the greatest advantage if the inbreeding coefficient is –1, as all matings generate heterozygotes.
claims.source: The wtf driver has the greatest advantage if the inbreeding coefficient is –1, as all matings generate heterozygotes.
claims.evidence: This is a result from population genetic modeling.

claims.claim: The wtf driver increases in frequency over generations of sexual reproduction under all conditions where some heterozygotes form, even when the driver starts at very low frequencies.
claims.source: Under all other conditions, including the range of inbreeding coefficients we measured experimentally in S. pombe natural isolates, some heterozygotes form. The wtf driver thus increases in frequency over generations of sexual reproduction, even when the driver starts at very low (anything greater than 0) frequencies (Figure 3A and B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, see Materials and methods) (Crow, 1991).
claims.evidence: This is a result from population genetic modeling supported by figures and a citation.

claims.claim: wtf drivers can spread under the modeled conditions if some non-same-clone mating occurs, even if it is infrequent.
claims.source: This model predicts that wtf drivers can spread under the modeled conditions if some non-same-clone mating occurs, even if it is infrequent.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion from population genetic modeling.

claims.claim: Inbreeding can slow the spread of meiotic drivers.
claims.source: This observation is consistent with previous theoretical analyses demonstrating that inbreeding can slow the spread of meiotic drivers (Martinossi-Allibert et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claims.claim: The probability of a driver's success was related to population size, with the driver most likely to be maintained in smaller populations and in populations with more random mating.
claims.source: Surprisingly, we found that the probability of a driver's success was related to population size, similar to the recent results of Martinossi-Allibert et al., 2021. Specifically, the driver was most likely to be maintained in the smaller populations and in populations with more random mating due to the driver's positive effect on its own allele transmission (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: This is a result from stochastic simulations supported by data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C and a citation.

claims.claim: Both fluorescent markers (GFP and mCherry) were lost from all experimental populations over time.
claims.source: We found that both fluorescent markers were lost from all our experimental populations over time (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A-B).
claims.evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A-B.

claims.claim: Loss of fluorescent markers was likely because insertion of the markers disrupted the ura4 gene and cells that excised the marker reverted the ura4 mutation and gained a fitness benefit.
claims.source: This was likely because insertion of the markers disrupted the ura4 gene and cells that excised the marker reverted the ura4 mutation and thereby gained a fitness benefit.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental design and observations.

claims.claim: In most cases, the number of mCherry-expressing cells increased at the expense of GFP-expressing cells over time in control populations.
claims.source: We found in most cases that the number of mCherry-expressing cells increased at the expense of GFP-expressing cells over time (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A-D).
claims.evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by data in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A-D.

claims.claim: The fitness cost of GFP in homozygotes was 0.234.
claims.source: We found that the fitness cost of the GFP in homozygotes was 0.234 (see Materials and methods).
claims.evidence: This is a calculated value from experimental data using maximum likelihood modeling.

claims.claim: The dominance of the GFP cost was 0.083.
claims.source: We found the dominance of the GFP cost was 0.083 (low fitness cost of GFP in GFP/mCherry heterozygotes).
claims.evidence: This is a calculated value from experimental data using maximum likelihood modeling.

claims.claim: In homothallic populations, wtf4 alleles spread in the population over several generations of sexual reproduction.
claims.source: In homothallic (inbreeding coefficient ~0.5) populations, we observed that wtf4 alleles spread in the population over several generations of sexual reproduction.
claims.evidence: This is an experimental finding from the experimental evolution experiments.

claims.claim: The driver spread faster when linked to mCherry than when linked to GFP, presumably due to fitness costs linked to GFP.
claims.source: The driver spread faster when linked to mCherry than when linked to GFP, presumably due to the aforementioned fitness costs linked to GFP (Figure 4B–C).
claims.evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by data in Figure 4B–C and inference about the cause.

claims.claim: In both cases, the rate of spread of the wtf4 allele was very close to the model's predictions assuming an inbreeding coefficient of 0.5.
claims.source: In both cases, the rate of spread of the allele was very close to our model's predictions if we assumed an inbreeding coefficient of 0.5 (black lines, Figure 4B–C) and differed considerably from the model's predictions assuming random mating (inbreeding coefficient = 0; gray lines, Figure 4B–C).
claims.evidence: This is a comparison of experimental data to model predictions shown in Figure 4B–C.

claims.claim: In mixed heterothallic populations, the wtf4 driver spread significantly faster than in homothallic cells.
claims.source: In the mixed heterothallic populations, the wtf4 driver spread significantly faster than in homothallic cells.
claims.evidence: This is an experimental finding from the experimental evolution experiments.

claims.claim: In generations 1–6 of heterothallic populations, the spread of wtf4 was very similar to that predicted by the model assuming random mating (inbreeding coefficient = 0).
claims.source: In generations 1–6, the spread of wtf4 was very similar to that predicted by our model if we assumed random mating (inbreeding coefficient = 0).
claims.evidence: This is a comparison of experimental data to model predictions.

claims.claim: Increasing heterozygote fitness beyond 0.51 decreased the fit of the data to the model.
claims.source: We found that increasing heterozygote fitness beyond 0.51 decreased the fit of our data to the model (Figure 5—figure supplement 2), suggesting wtf drivers do not gain additional benefits beyond killing spores bearing the alternate allele.
claims.evidence: This is a result from comparing experimental data to model predictions with varying parameters, shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: The population genetics model with driver heterozygote fitness at 0.51 is good at describing the spread of wtf4 in the experimental population, particularly in the first few generations.
claims.source: Overall, our results demonstrate that our population genetics model with driver heterozygote fitness at 0.51 is good at describing the spread of wtf4 in our experimental population, particularly in the first few generations.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion from comparing experimental data to model predictions.

claims.claim: Inbreeding coefficients near 0.5 slow, but do not stop, the spread of drivers in a population.
claims.source: Our results also confirm that inbreeding coefficients near 0.5 slow, but do not stop, the spread of drivers in a population.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion from experimental evolution experiments and modeling.

claims.claim: Meiotic drivers tend to accumulate linked deleterious alleles in nature.
claims.source: Meiotic drivers tend to accumulate linked deleterious alleles in nature (Atlan et al., 2004; Dyer et al., 2007; Finnegan et al., 2019; Fishman and Saunders, 2008; Higgins et al., 2018; Lyon, 2003; Olds-Clarke, 1997; Schimenti et al., 2005; Unckless et al., 2015; Wilkinson and Fry, 2001; Wu, 1983).
claims.evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claims.claim: Driving alleles in the Sk isolate are linked to a chromosomal translocation that decreases fitness in heterozygotes.
claims.source: While the linkage of individual drivers to deleterious alleles in S. pombe has not been extensively investigated, driving alleles in the Sk isolate are linked to a chromosomal translocation that decreases fitness in heterozygotes (Zanders et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claims.claim: Chromosomal rearrangements involving chromosome 3, which houses most wtf genes, are common in S. pombe.
claims.source: Similar chromosomal rearrangements involving chromosome 3, which houses most wtf genes, are common in S. pombe, so it is likely drivers are frequently linked to rearrangements (Bowen et al., 2003; Brown et al., 2011; Avelar et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: In the absence of additional linked costs, wtf drivers are predicted to spread in a population at all initial frequencies greater than 0.
claims.source: We found that, in the absence of additional linked costs, wtf drivers are predicted to spread in a population at all initial frequencies greater than 0 (Figure 5A).
claims.evidence: This is a result from population genetic modeling shown in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: When the driver is burdened by additional fitness costs, it can still spread in a population, but must start at a higher initial frequency.
claims.source: When the driver is burdened by additional fitness costs, it can still spread in a population. Importantly, however, as the fitness costs of linked deleterious alleles increase, the driver must start at a higher initial frequency to spread.
claims.evidence: This is a result from population genetic modeling.

claims.claim: If fitness costs are recessive or close to recessive, a driver can invade at low frequencies in a randomly mating population, but would require a higher initial frequency to spread in an inbreeding population.
claims.source: If the fitness costs are recessive or close to recessive (dominance coefficient h near 0), a driver can invade at low frequencies in a randomly mating population, but a driver would require a higher initial frequency to spread in an inbreeding population (inbreeding coefficients > 0; Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This is a result from population genetic modeling shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: If fitness costs are partially dominant (50% dominance), the drivers require a higher initial frequency to spread, even with random mating.
claims.source: If the fitness costs are partially dominant (50% dominance), the drivers require a higher initial frequency to spread, even with random mating (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This is a result from population genetic modeling shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: Linked costs could limit the maintenance of a driver particularly in populations that inbreed in finite populations where drift can occur.
claims.source: In finite populations in which drift can occur, we also observed that linked costs could limit the maintenance of a driver particularly in populations that inbreed (inbreeding coefficients > 0; Figure 5—figure supplement 1C,D).
claims.evidence: This is a result from stochastic simulations shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C,D.

claims.claim: The cost of the deleterious allele is fixed, but the benefit a driver gains from drive is frequency dependent.
claims.source: This is in line with previous modeling and can be explained because the cost of the deleterious allele is fixed, but the benefit a driver gains from drive is frequency dependent (Drury et al., 2017; Martinossi-Allibert et al., 2021; Nauta and Hoekstra, 1993).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: The driver failed to spread when the initial frequency was less than 0.25 in experimental populations.
claims.source: Consistent with the predictions of our model, we observed in the experimental populations that the driver failed to spread when the initial frequency was less than 0.25 (Figure 5B).
claims.evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by data in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: When the wtf4:GFP allele was found in roughly half of the population, it could spread when the inbreeding coefficient was low but decreased in frequency when the inbreeding coefficient was increased.
claims.source: When the wtf4:GFP allele was found in roughly half of the population, it could spread when the inbreeding coefficient was low but decreased in frequency when the inbreeding coefficient was increased (Figure 5B).
claims.evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by data in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: Experimental analyses are consistent with the predictions of the model and show that both inbreeding and linked deleterious alleles can impede the spread of a wtf meiotic driver.
claims.source: Altogether, our experimental analyses are consistent with the predictions of our model and show that both inbreeding and linked deleterious alleles can impede the spread of a wtf meiotic driver.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion from comparing experimental data to model predictions.

claims.claim: Genetic variation within S. pombe is limited.
claims.source: Although genetic variation within S. pombe is limited, past studies found variation in mating efficiency and uncovered genetic diversity of the mating-type locus (Jeffares et al., 2015; Nieuwenhuis et al., 2018; Rhind et al., 2011; Singh and Klar, 2002).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: Past studies found variation in mating efficiency in S. pombe.
claims.source: Although genetic variation within S. pombe is limited, past studies found variation in mating efficiency and uncovered genetic diversity of the mating-type locus (Jeffares et al., 2015; Nieuwenhuis et al., 2018; Rhind et al., 2011; Singh and Klar, 2002).

results.result: Natural variation in inbreeding propensity exists among S. pombe isolates. Using fluorescence microscopy and genetic assays, the authors measured inbreeding coefficients ranging from near 0 (random mating) in isolates like Sk to ~0.5-0.6 in the lab strain Sp. Cell density affects inbreeding coefficients, with lower densities leading to higher inbreeding in both Sp and Sk isolates.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C47-C54 provide converging evidence from two independent assays (microscopy and genetic markers) showing consistent inbreeding coefficients across isolates. The microscopy assay was validated with heterothallic controls showing random mating (F=-0.05, C48). The density effect (C52-C54) is well-controlled with heterothallic populations showing random mating at all densities, demonstrating the effect is specific to homothallic strains.

results.result: The Sk isolate exhibits distinct mating timing patterns compared to Sp. At low density (0.25×), Sk cells divided significantly more (p<0.005) before mating, with most mating occurring at generation 4, whereas Sp mated primarily at generations 2-3. At standard density (1×), Sk mating timing shifted to generations 2-3 like Sp, but sibling mating decreased from 56% to 10%.
results.evaluation: Claims C55-C62 are supported by time-lapse microscopy data with statistical testing (C55). The density-dependent shift in Sk mating patterns (C61-C62) provides mechanistic insight consistent with reduced mating-type switching. The observations are internally consistent and supported by quantitative data across multiple experiments.

results.result: A ~5 kb insertion of nested Tf transposon sequences was discovered in the Sk mating-type region near the double-strand break site. This insertion was confirmed by PCR and found in at least one other isolate (FY28981) that also exhibits more random mating.
results.evaluation: Claims C58-C60 and C116 describe a genomic finding confirmed by two independent methods (mate-pair sequencing analysis and PCR). The presence of the same insertion in another randomly-mating isolate (C60) provides correlative support, though the authors appropriately note this insertion doesn't explain all mating variation (C118).

results.result: The data are consistent with a model where less frequent mating-type switching in Sk contributes to more random mating. The authors propose the transposon insertion could contribute to reduced DNA break formation and decreased switching, building on prior observations by Singh and Klar (2002).
results.evaluation: Claims C113-C117 represent a plausible mechanistic model but lack direct evidence. The authors acknowledge they did not directly measure switching rates (using mating as a proxy instead). While the model is consistent with observations (C113), the causal link between the insertion and switching frequency remains speculative (C117). Direct measurement of switching rates would be needed to support this result.

results.result: Available sexual partners affect mating phenotypes. In mixed Sk/Sp populations, Sk cells maintained low sibling mating (9.2%), while Sp sibling mating decreased significantly from 56.8% to 29.7% (p=0.04). Sk/Sp matings produced significantly longer zygotes/asci than isogenic matings.
results.evaluation: Claims C67-C70 demonstrate partner-dependent effects with statistical support (C69). The maintenance of Sk's low sibling mating in mixed populations (C68) and the change in Sp behavior (C69) are well-documented. The zygote length observation (C70) provides additional phenotypic evidence, though its mechanistic significance is unclear.

results.result: The Sk isolate displays tremendous diversity in ascus size and shape, with ~25% of zygotes/asci exceeding 15 μm (some >30 μm), compared to the typical 10-15 μm range in most isolates. Long shmoos were produced only in response to opposite mating-type cells, not nitrogen starvation alone.
results.evaluation: Claims C63-C66 describe well-documented morphological observations with quantitative measurements (C65) and appropriate controls (C66). The specificity of long shmoo formation to mating-type recognition (C66) is properly controlled. These observations are descriptive but well-supported.

results.result: Population genetic modeling predicts wtf drivers can spread under all inbreeding conditions where some heterozygotes form (F<1), even from very low initial frequencies. The driver has greatest advantage at F=-1 (complete outcrossing) but increases in frequency at all measured S. pombe inbreeding coefficients, consistent with previous theoretical work showing inbreeding slows but doesn't prevent driver spread.
results.evaluation: Claims C71-C74 present modeling results that are mathematically sound and consistent with established theory (C74 cites Martinossi-Allibert et al., 2021). The model appropriately uses empirically measured parameters (98% drive, fitness 0.51 for heterozygotes) from prior work. The conclusion that drivers can spread at all F<1 follows logically from the model assumptions.

results.result: Stochastic simulations incorporating genetic drift showed that driver success probability was related to population size, with drivers most likely maintained in smaller populations and those with more random mating.
results.evaluation: Claim C75 describes results from Wright-Fisher simulations supported by Figure 3—figure supplement 1C. The finding is consistent with recent work (Martinossi-Allibert et al., 2021) and represents a counterintuitive result about drift effects on driver dynamics. The simulation approach is appropriate for exploring stochastic effects.

results.result: Fluorescent markers were lost from experimental populations over time, likely due to excision reverting the ura4 disruption. GFP showed a fitness cost of 0.234 in homozygotes with low dominance (h=0.083), calculated using maximum likelihood fitting to control population data.
results.evaluation: Claims C76-C80 identify and quantify a technical issue in the experimental system. The inference about marker loss mechanism (C77) is reasonable given the integration method. The fitness cost quantification (C79-C80) uses appropriate maximum likelihood methods on control data, though the authors acknowledge one exception where this cost wasn't observed (heterothallic wtf4/wtf4 populations).

results.result: Experimental evolution confirmed model predictions: wtf4 spread in homothallic populations (F~0.5) at rates matching model predictions for F=0.5, and spread faster in heterothallic populations (F~0) matching random mating predictions for generations 1-6. The driver spread faster when linked to mCherry than GFP due to GFP-associated fitness costs.
results.evaluation: Claims C81-C85 demonstrate strong agreement between experimental data and model predictions across multiple conditions. The comparison uses empirically measured parameters and shows good fit particularly in early generations (C83, C85). The GFP cost effect (C82) is consistent with the measured fitness parameters (C79-C80). Later generation deviations are acknowledged and attributed to marker loss.

results.result: The population genetics model with heterozygote fitness of 0.51 accurately describes wtf4 spread in experimental populations, particularly in early generations. Testing alternative fitness values showed that increasing heterozygote fitness beyond 0.51 decreased model fit, suggesting wtf drivers gain no additional benefits beyond spore killing. The results confirm inbreeding coefficients near 0.5 slow but don't stop driver spread.
results.evaluation: Claims C86-C88 represent rigorous model validation. Testing alternative fitness parameters (C86) and finding decreased fit provides evidence against additional driver benefits. The conclusion about inbreeding effects (C88) is supported by both modeling and experimental data. The model-experiment agreement validates both approaches.

results.result: Modeling the effects of linked deleterious alleles shows drivers can spread from any initial frequency >0 without additional costs, but require higher initial frequencies as linked costs increase. The effect depends on dominance: recessive costs (h~0) allow low-frequency invasion in random mating but require higher frequencies with inbreeding; partially dominant costs (h=0.5) require higher initial frequencies even with random mating. In finite populations with drift, linked costs particularly limit driver maintenance in inbreeding populations.
results.evaluation: Claims C92-C97 present systematic modeling of linked cost effects with appropriate parameter exploration. The results are consistent with previous modeling (C97 cites supporting work) and the explanation about fixed costs vs. frequency-dependent benefits is sound. The modeling appropriately considers both deterministic and stochastic scenarios.

results.result: Experimental tests with the GFP-linked wtf4 driver confirmed model predictions: the driver failed to spread from initial frequencies <0.25, and at ~50% initial frequency could spread at low inbreeding but decreased at high inbreeding. These results demonstrate both inbreeding and linked deleterious alleles can impede driver spread.
results.evaluation: Claims C98-C100 provide experimental validation of model predictions about linked costs and inbreeding effects. The experiments appropriately manipulate both initial frequency and inbreeding coefficient (via cell density), and results match model predictions. This represents strong integration of theory and experiment.

results.result: All studied homothallic S. pombe natural isolates underwent some non-same-clone mating, with some isolates like Sk showing considerable outcrossing (F~0). Sp mating efficiency was ~40%, consistent with previous work, with variable efficiencies across isolates. These findings support that homothallism is compatible with outcrossing.
results.evaluation: Claims C104-C109 summarize key experimental findings with appropriate citations to previous work (C104-C105). The observation that all homothallic isolates show some outcrossing (C107) is well-documented, and the Sk example (C108) demonstrates this can be substantial. The conclusion about homothallism compatibility (C109) is appropriately supported by both current data and cited prior work.

results.result: Integration of modeling and experimental results shows observed S. pombe inbreeding coefficients slow but don't halt wtf driver spread (except with low frequency and linked deleterious alleles). Experimental results closely matched model predictions, suggesting the model captures all critical parameters. The variation in mating phenotypes indicates driver spread rates will vary between S. pombe populations.
results.evaluation: Claims C143-C148 synthesize the major findings. The close model-experiment agreement (C145) across multiple conditions supports the inference that critical parameters are captured (C146). The conclusions about inbreeding effects (C143-C144) and population variation (C148) are well-supported by the combined theoretical and experimental evidence.

results.result: S. pombe is reported to rarely outcross yet harbors many meiotic drivers, challenging the assumption that drivers are unsuccessful in rarely outcrossing species. Very little is known about S. pombe ecology and outcrossing frequency, and precise levels of same-clone mating in the presence of potential outcrossing partners had not been formally reported.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C2, C16, C19, C28, C32, and C39 establish the paradox motivating this study. These are well-supported by citations to previous work documenting both the presumed rarity of outcrossing and the presence of multiple drivers. The statement about lack of quantitative data (C32) appropriately identifies a knowledge gap the study addresses.

results.result: Nanopore sequencing analysis revealed an approximate 3:1 excess of the h+ allele at the mat1 locus in isolate FY29033. This mating-type bias is predicted to facilitate non-same-clone mating.
results.evaluation: Claims C122-C123 present a genomic observation with appropriate statistical analysis (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C shows Fisher's exact test results). The inference that mating-type bias facilitates outcrossing (C123) is logical and consistent with cited prior work on atypical mating-type loci.

results.result: The study does not address actual outcrossing frequency in wild S. pombe populations. Previous genomic estimates of outcrossing rates assume Mendelian transmission and recombination rates matching pure Sp, but these assumptions are inconsistent with empirical data on meiotic drive and recombination suppression, likely leading to underestimation of true outcrossing rates.
results.evaluation: Claims C124-C128 appropriately acknowledge study limitations (C124) and critically evaluate prior work. The critique of genomic estimates (C126-C128) is well-supported by citations showing violations of key assumptions. The inference about underestimation (C128) follows logically from the identified assumption violations.

results.result: Heterozygosity for wtf drivers may not require outcrossing between distantly related strains because wtf genes evolve extremely rapidly through non-allelic gene conversion and repeat expansion/contraction. Despite low overall genetic diversity in S. pombe (<1%), wtf genes are largely distinct between isolates (25-38 genes per isolate, with dramatic differences even at the same locus). Small sequence changes can create new drivers, and when novel driver mutations mate with cells lacking them, drive can occur in the resulting heterozygote.
results.evaluation: Claims C129-C141 present a well-supported model for driver evolution and maintenance. The rapid evolution of wtf genes (C130-C138) is documented by multiple citations. The inference that heterozygosity can arise within relatively homogeneous populations (C129, C141) follows logically from the documented rapid evolution and lack of cross-protection between different wtf sequences (C139).

results.result: Background on meiotic drivers: they break Mendel's law to achieve >50% transmission from heterozygotes by manipulating gametogenesis. Drivers rely on outcrossing because they gain advantage in heterozygotes. While outcrossing can purge deleterious alleles, it can also promote spread of selfish genes like drivers. Inbreeding is thought to inhibit driver spread, predicting drivers should be unsuccessful in rarely outcrossing species.
results.evaluation: Claims C7-C15 provide well-established background information, all supported by appropriate citations to foundational work in the field. These claims accurately represent current understanding of meiotic drive systems and set up the paradox addressed by the study.

results.result: Background on wtf drivers in S. pombe: The genome contains numerous wtf meiotic drive genes (4-14 drivers per isolate, plus 8-17 suppressors). Each driver encodes both poison and antidote proteins. In wtf4, the poison assembles into toxic aggregates packaged into all spores, while the antidote co-assembles with poison only in spores inheriting the driver, likely neutralizing it via vacuolar trafficking. This results in ~50% spore death and >90% driver transmission from heterozygotes.
results.evaluation: Claims C40-C46 summarize well-established characteristics of wtf drivers from prior work by this research group and others. results.result: The results are consistent with previous empirical and modeling studies showing meiotic drivers tend to accumulate linked deleterious alleles that can hitchhike with drivers, reducing their spread and potentially leading to stable intermediate frequencies. In S. pombe, drivers in the Sk isolate are linked to a chromosomal translocation, and such rearrangements involving chromosome 3 (which houses most wtf genes) are common. Inbreeding can be selected when drivers are recessive lethal.

results.result: The S. pombe experimental evolution system could be used to model sex-ratio-distorting drivers (by linking drivers to mating-type loci in heterothallic populations) or explore complex multi-locus drive systems with multiple drivers and suppressors. This tool may provide insights into natural drivers and help explore evolutionary trajectories of artificial gene drive systems.
